item.title: FOCUS I What is parentification?
item.description: Eve was an adult when she realised she grew up in a home where child-parent roles were reversed. Eve and her siblings were in school when they began taking on adult responsibilities at home, due to their mother’s declining mental health.
item.content:encoded:
Eve was an adult when she realised she grew up in a home where child-parent roles were reversed.

Eve and her siblings were in school when they began taking on adult responsibilities at home, due to their mother’s declining mental health.

The now-51-year-old from Sydney/Gadigal lands recalls her mother spending most days in bed due to severe depression and her father becoming increasingly absent.

“Mum would leave instructions for getting dinner ready and she’d leave the stuff in the fridge,” says Eve, not her real name.

“Then as time went on, we were basically running the household, doing everything from cooking, laundry, cleaning, shopping, all of that.”

As well as doing physical labour, Eve, who was a young teenager when she first took on these responsibilities, says she also became an emotional support for her mother, who had experienced childhood sexual trauma.

“Mum would talk to me about what had happened to her [as a child] and she was basically using me as kind of like a quasi-counsellor, it was really inappropriate.”

Eve says at the time she wasn’t able to process what was happening, she just “got on with it”.

It wasn’t until she studied to become a social worker that she came across the term parentification and finally “felt validated”.

Parentification is a psychological term used to describe a role reversal where children have parental-level responsibilities above what is deemed developmentally appropriate, according to Rachael Sharman, a lecturer and researcher in psychology, specialising in child/adolescent development.

She says people can experience different forms of parentification and at varying degrees of severity.

“I used to work in child protection, and this was something that we looked out for quite a lot,” says Sharman, based on the Sunshine Coast/Kabi Kabi lands.

“[One day] we were talking to a mother, we noticed her six-year-old daughter come home from school, jump up to the kitchen bench, get herself something to eat and drink, then proceeded to wipe down all the benches and table, make the baby a bottle and feed the baby.”

Children who are parentified take on emotional and instrumental responsibilities before their brain is developmentally ready, but also before they are ready emotionally, according to Deirdre Brandner, a child and adolescent psychologist, based in Melbourne/Naarm.

But she believes emotional parentification is more damaging, because the child is managing the emotions of the parents.

“This is when kids are the parents’ confidant or they’re the emotional regulator for the parents, [for example] ‘Dad looks like he’s stressed, I need to go and do this to make sure he’s OK.’”

Brander says international studies, including a large, nationally representative study from Poland in 2021, suggest “up to one in three young people, particularly adolescents” experience emotional parentification.

But she says the signs of parentification in children are often “subtle because people see these kids as mature, as helpful, as capable, as highly competent”.

Hyper vigilance to other people’s moods, even peers at school

Feeling responsible for adults’ wellbeing

Sharman says “it can manifest quite differently” depending on the age of the person and the severity of the parentification.

“What we typically see is around the age of 16 to 25, that later adolescence, they start to work out that something’s not right.”

A life of ‘hyper independence and responsibility’

As an adult, Eve says she has found it difficult to say no to extra responsibilities, put her own needs first, while being hyper independent.

“I’ve never had that experience of parents turning up to stuff, going on a university tour with me when I was at the end of year 12, or getting my driver’s licence,” she says.

She also found herself in an intimate relationship that mirrored the unhealthy family dynamic she grew up with.

“Even though [ending that relationship] has been incredibly difficult, I can look back on that now and understand why I went into it,” she says.

But there were some positives. Eve says she is a more “compassionate and empathetic person” and credits her successful 20-year career in the public mental health sector to her childhood experiences.

Children who are parentified take on emotional and instrumental responsibilities before their brain is developmentally ready. Picture: www.childfocusnj.org

item.title: BEHIND THE NEWS I An alliance of equals
item.description: When Fiji signed the Ocean of Peace Alliance with Australia last month, it crossed a historic threshold. For the first time since independence, Fiji entered a formal mutual defence treaty which commits both nations to come to each other’s aid in times of greatest need. It is, by any measure, a landmark agreement. The treaty elevates the Vuvale relationship beyond development assistance and militar
item.content:encoded:
When Fiji signed the Ocean of Peace Alliance with Australia last month, it crossed a historic threshold. For the first time since independence, Fiji entered a formal mutual defence treaty which commits both nations to come to each other’s aid in times of greatest need.

It is, by any measure, a landmark agreement. The treaty elevates the Vuvale relationship beyond development assistance and military cooperation into something far more consequential: a reciprocal security commitment. Australia describes it as one of its formal alliances, while Fiji presents it as a partnership built on shared sovereignty and regional stability. The language is reassuring, the symbolism powerful. But behind the ceremony lies a serious question that deserves public discussion.

If Australia were attacked tomorrow, what exactly could Fiji contribute?

This is not a question of loyalty. It is a question of capability.

Mutual defence treaties carry enormous political weight because they imply reciprocal obligations. The Australia–Fiji agreement states that both countries will come to one another’s assistance during their “times of greatest need”, reflecting the collective defence principle found in many military alliances around the world.

Yet reciprocity between unequal partners has always been complicated.

Australia possesses one of the Indo-Pacific’s most capable militaries: blue-water naval vessels, fighter aircraft, submarines, cyber capabilities and sophisticated intelligence networks. Its defence budget runs into tens of billions of dollars annually. Fiji’s Republic of Fiji Military Forces (RFMF), by contrast, has traditionally been structured around territorial security, peacekeeping and humanitarian response rather than conventional warfare.

The imbalance is obvious. An attack on Fiji would likely see Australia providing ships, aircraft, logistics, surveillance and intelligence almost immediately. But if Australia faced a comparable threat, Fiji cannot realistically offer equivalent military power.

That does not make the treaty meaningless. It simply raises the question of what reciprocity actually looks like.

International treaties often treat states as juridically equal regardless of their size. A country of one million people signs alongside a nation of 27 million with equal sovereign status. Legally, that principle is important.

Operationally, however, equality becomes more nuanced.

Consider the hypothetical scenario that has lingered quietly since the treaty was announced. Australia comes under military attack. Its northern approaches are contested. Maritime supply routes require protection. Would Fiji dispatch troops? Patrol vessels? Engineers? Medical teams? Intelligence officers? Or would its contribution be largely symbolic — a political declaration of support alongside specialised assistance where possible?

The treaty does not erase the reality that Fiji’s armed forces were never designed to fight Australia’s wars.

There is another way of viewing security altogether.

For decades, Fiji has earned international respect not because of overwhelming military strength, but because of disciplined peacekeepers. From the Middle East to Africa, Fijian soldiers have built a reputation for professionalism under United Nations mandates. Disaster response has become another defining strength, with the RFMF regularly deployed during cyclones, floods and regional emergencies.

Modern security is increasingly multidimensional. Cybersecurity, humanitarian assistance, maritime surveillance, illegal fishing, disaster logistics and infrastructure resilience are now as strategically important as tanks and missiles. Australia’s engagement with Pacific countries has increasingly focused on these areas rather than preparing island states for conventional interstate warfare.

If that is the true intention of the alliance, then public expectations should reflect it.

Because when ordinary citizens hear the phrase “mutual defence”, many understandably imagine soldiers defending each other’s territory in battle. The practical reality may be far broader — and far less dramatic.

The treaty also arrives during a period of intensifying geopolitical competition.

Australia has been strengthening defence partnerships across the Pacific, including agreements with Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and now Fiji, as strategic rivalry between major powers becomes increasingly pronounced.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has consistently argued that Fiji’s foreign policy remains one of friendship with all and enemies with none. The Ocean of Peace concept itself seeks to place Pacific priorities — not great-power rivalry — at the centre of regional security.

That aspiration is admirable. But bilateral defence alliances inevitably create perceptions. Whether intended or not, they are interpreted by larger powers as strategic alignment.

For Fiji, the challenge is maintaining strategic autonomy while benefiting from closer security cooperation. The stronger the alliance becomes, the more important it is for Suva to clearly articulate where its obligations begin and where they end.

None of this is an argument against the treaty.

Australia has long been Fiji’s closest security partner. The two countries cooperate extensively on maritime surveillance, military training, humanitarian response and peacekeeping. Formalising that relationship may well enhance regional stability and improve Fiji’s own preparedness for natural disasters and emerging security threats.

But democratic oversight requires asking difficult questions before a crisis, not during one.

What constitutes an “attack” that triggers mutual assistance?

Is military deployment automatic, or does each Parliament retain discretion?

What forms of assistance satisfy Fiji’s obligations — combat forces, logistics, intelligence or humanitarian support?

Would Fiji be expected to contribute beyond the Pacific if Australia were involved in a wider regional conflict?

item.title: YOUTH I Youths connect to celebrate
item.description: YOUNG people from across Navosa were given a platform to connect and celebrate as the Navosa Youth Festival brought together sport, entertainment, information and community engagement. The festival formed part of Fiji’s national celebration of International Youth Day and included booths where organisations and businesses shared information and services with young people from the province.
item.content:encoded:
YOUNG people from across Navosa were given a platform to connect and celebrate as the Navosa Youth Festival brought together sport, entertainment, information and community engagement.

The festival formed part of Fiji’s national celebration of International Youth Day and included booths where organisations and businesses shared information and services with young people from the province.

Rugby matches, entertainment and other activities added to the celebrations, creating a space where young people could take part, discover opportunities and connect with organisations working in their communities.

During the celebration, Youth and Sports Minister Jese Saukuru officially handed over gym equipment to Navosa Central College, which will also be used by the Navosa Rugby Union.

For Mr Saukuru, the festival represented more than a day of activities.

“This is your day, this is your platform and this is your opportunity,” he told young people from Navosa and Nadroga.

Different backgrounds, shared aspirations

International Youth Day is observed globally on August 12 each year.

This year’s theme, “Different Contexts Common Aspirations”, reflects the different experiences of young people while recognising the aspirations they share.

Saukuru said young people came from different islands, villages, schools, communities, cultures and backgrounds. They also faced different challenges.

But beneath those differences were common hopes and dreams.

“They want dignity, they want opportunities, they want quality educational skills, they want decent employment and meaningful livelihoods,” he said.

Young people also wanted to participate in decisions affecting their lives, to be healthy, safe and respected, and to be heard.

For the Minister, young people should not be viewed only as future leaders.

He acknowledged the contribution young Fijians were already making in rural and maritime communities, towns and cities, schools, workplaces, sporting fields and youth clubs.

“We see young people stepping forward and lead community activities, we see young people learning new skills, we see them taking part in sport, we see young entrepreneurs creating opportunities for themselves and others and we see young people speaking up on issues that matter to their communities,” he said.

Although individual contributions could sometimes appear small, Saukuru said they made a difference when brought together.

“Our young people are not just the leaders of tomorrow, you are leaders and contributors today,” he said.

That belief sits at the centre of the Ministry of Youth and Sports’ approach, with youth development and sports development serving as two important ways of reaching young people.

Saukuru said youth development was about more than organising programs.

“It is about creating pathways. It is about building confidence; it is about developing leadership. It is about giving young people skills, knowledge, values, and opportunities.”

Sport, he said, also carried lessons beyond competition.

“It teaches discipline, it teaches teamwork, it teaches resilience, it teaches respect, it teaches young people how to win with humility and how to lose with dignity.”

The Navosa Youth Festival was also a fulfilment of a request made during Saukuru’s visit to Nukuilau Village.

During that visit, he was asked whether a youth festival could be held in Navosa.

“My answer was a simple yes and today, we are here,” he said.

The festival turned that conversation into an event bringing young people together through sports, cultural activities, skills training, exhibitions and community activities.

For Saukuru, such festivals provide spaces where young people can feel valued and discover their talents, while communities can begin conversations about difficult issues affecting them.

“These festivals are much more than sporting competitions,” he said.

They bring together sport, culture, leadership, awareness, community engagement and conversations around issues affecting young people.

item.title: REFLECTION I The story behind the enchanted forest
item.description: This poem is inspired by my garden project. I decided to create a minature garden, based upon the childhood charm of a Faiiryland home. I adorned the garden with solar lights to twinkle under the midnight sky and provide light by the garden path to the creatures who happily make my garden their enchanted home.
item.content:encoded:
This poem is inspired by my garden project. I decided to create a minature garden, based upon the childhood charm of a Faiiryland home.

I adorned the garden with solar lights to twinkle under the midnight sky and provide light by the garden path to the creatures who happily make my garden their enchanted home.

Alas, my hope of seeing a fairy has not transpired as yet but I have witnessed creatures small and sacred in my garden, which has been an enchanting encounter.

I have seen earthworms keep warm in the soil.

I have seen butterflies dance around the buds and blooms.

I have seen dragonflies float by on wings crafted as fine as lace

I have witnessed my sunflowers turn their gaze towards the sun

I have witnessed my wand plants (pink orchids) grow tall and sway in the winds. My vision is that one day, they will all be as tall as the solar light poles and because I have decorated my garden with this most graceful plant, I hope to see blooms when the Season arrives. The tall stems that sway gentle in the breeze is indeed, my vision of an enchanted garden.

I have seen frog families seek refuge amongst my garden decor.

I have witnessed bees extract pollen from blooms

My farm-acy is bountiful with herbs and vegetable yields for a dry Season

I have propagated blooms planted by my father two decades earlier and the first bloom opened bright and beautiful on his birthday. It was one of the most magical moments I have ever witnessed and to this day, remains an enchanting memory.

Indeed, to bear witness to the serene work of Nature in my garden is an enchanting experience.

Any person that seeks to align their labour of love with Nature, will undertake every effort to ensure that the earth is aware of their dedication to Her care and as a reward, one’s yield will be bountiful.

Most of the creatures small and sacred in my garden have provisions for shelter and safety but alas, I noted that the birds did not consider my garden a home as yet.

I installed a minature pond with a wooden walk-way and each morning, I would watch in wonder as they arrived at dawn for a bird-bath or to quench their thirst.

Alas, my pets were not too impressed by their presence and considered the pond as their water tub so I had to remove the pond in haste and spare the birds any harm.

My new initiative will be from experience. I intend to install a bird stand with a minature pond atop it, so the birds can bathe in peace!

Still no fairies in sight but what an enchanting

sight under the sunlight has Nature presented to me.

The knowledge I have acquired is invaluable.

1. Whispering positive words to plants to see them bloom

2. Utilising natural fertilisers to guide the growth of plants

3. Decorating my garden with antique decor items no longer in usage

4. Placing compost buckets around the garden and utilising food peels from the kitchen so that all plants receive energy to grow in their time. To witness the power of energy in Nature is a true experience in science.

Some plants share energy with other plants.

The poet’s garden at home. Picture: SUPPLIED

item.title: ENTREPRENEURSHIP I Turning creativity into opportunity
item.description: FOR women in rural Navosa, the daily village life often revolves around household responsibilities and yaqona farming. But a two-day training program at the Nasau Youth Training Centre has offered a glimpse of another possibility, turning creativity and practical skills into income.
item.content:encoded:
FOR women in rural Navosa, the daily village life often revolves around household responsibilities and yaqona farming.

But a two-day training program at the Nasau Youth Training Centre has offered a glimpse of another possibility, turning creativity and practical skills into income.

The tie-dye and soap-making training brought young people together to learn skills they could use to support themselves and their families.

For Raijeli Naceva of Nausori Highlands in the district of Namataku, Navosa, the experience opened her mind to possibilities she had not previously considered.

You know life in the village, most of us women do household work and our income is from yaqona farming,” she said.

Naceva said being part of the training has shown her that tie-dye and soap making could become more than activities learnt during a program.

“Being part of the tie-dye and soap making training that was held at Nasau has really opened my mind to the possibility of going into a tie-dye business or soap making to support my family,” she said.

The training was part of activities leading up to the Navosa Youth and Sports Festival 2026, held from August 13 to 14 at Vatureba Grounds, Navosa.

The program gave young people an opportunity to learn practical skills while exploring their creativity and considering how those skills could be developed into small income-generating opportunities.

For Naceva, the training also challenged her expectations about how difficult the skills would be to learn.

“I didn’t know that it would be so easy to make soap or to dye materials,” she said.

The experience allowed her to acquire a new skill and receive certification for what she had learnt.

The program, according to the Ministry of Youth and Sports, was designed to help young people develop practical skills they could use to produce and market their own tie-dye products.

It also encouraged participants to explore entrepreneurship and creativity while building skills that could contribute to sustainable livelihoods.

For young people in rural communities, the training provided an opportunity to strengthen their capacity for greater self-reliance and economic participation within their communities.

Youth and Sports Minister Jese Saukuru said he had the privilege of handing over 42 certificates to young people from Navosa who completed the two-day tie-dye and soap-making training.

For him, the certificates represented more than the completion of a training program.

“These are more than just certificates, they represent new skills, new confidence, hopefully new opportunities for our young people to earn an income and become more self-reliant,” Saukuru said.

The certificates marked the completion of two days of practical learning but for the participants, the knowledge gained could continue beyond the training centre.

For Amelia Namoumou of Vunaqoru, the training offered a new perspective on what could be achieved through learning a practical skill.

She said the experience had widened her horizon and shown her what she could achieve with a little training.

Namoumou was grateful to the Ministry of Youth and Sports for giving her the opportunity to participate, particularly because the skills she learnt could help her generate an income in the future.

Her experience reflected one of the key aims of the training, to give young people practical knowledge that could open possibilities beyond what they already know.

The training was not simply about learning how to make soap or create tie-dye products.

For participants such as Naceva and Namoumou, it was an introduction to skills that could potentially become part of their future livelihoods.

The Ministry of Youth and Sports said activities such as the training were aimed at supporting and empowering young people with skills that could help them build confidence, become more self-reliant and create opportunities for themselves and their communities.

The emphasis was on practical learning, creativity and the possibility of turning skills into small income-generating opportunities.

Participants listen to their trainer during their soap-making session. Picture: MINISTRY OF YOUTH AND SPORTS

The tie-dye and soap-making training empowers young people to learn skills to support themselves. Picture: SUPPLIED by Ministry

The two-day training program at the Nasau Youth Training Centre has offered a glimpse of another possibility, turning creativity and practical skills into income. Picture: MINISTRY OF YOUTH AND SPORTS

item.title: COMMUNITY SERVICE I Church steps into national service
item.description: From today until August 29, something unusual will be taking place across Fiji. In 202 venues, from the main centres to remote communities and the scattered islands, church halls, community spaces and other meeting places will become points of contact for a national campaign that seeks to bring together faith, health and civic responsibility.
item.content:encoded:
From today until August 29, something unusual will be taking place across Fiji.

In 202 venues, from the main centres to remote communities and the scattered islands, church halls, community spaces and other meeting places will become points of contact for a national campaign that seeks to bring together faith, health and civic responsibility.

For many people, the first encounter may have little to do with a pulpit. They may come for a health check.

They may stop to taste a health juice or sample a healthier meal. Others may simply be curious about what is happening in their neighbourhood.

That is how the Seventh-day Adventist Church hopes Fiji for Christ will meet people — not only through nightly evangelistic meetings, but through practical acts of service that touch everyday life.

For two weeks, free health checks and health-awareness activities will be offered at outreach booths around the country. In towns, cities, settlements and rural communities, the campaign will bring together church volunteers, health workers and community members.

Then, each evening, a different kind of conversation will begin. Before the main program, a 15-minute civic and public health segment will address issues that have become increasingly difficult for Fiji to ignore — HIV and AIDS, teenage pregnancy, drug abuse and trafficking, family concerns and crime.

Police officers, health officials and family-life specialists will contribute to the sessions, giving the program a distinctly community-focused character.

The message is simple: a healthy society requires more than sermons. It requires people willing to talk about the problems affecting their homes, their children and their communities.

Hope FM and Hope TV, broadcasting around the clock from their Suvavou headquarters, will extend that conversation beyond the physical venues. For the church, these activities form part of its largest evangelistic undertaking in Fiji, carried out under the Fiji for Christ banner.

“At the core of Fiji for Christ is a message of divine love for every Fijian,” says the church’s Sabbath School and Church Planting director, Pastor Maika Vakamelei.

“And we invite every willing heart to join this life-saving exercise from wherever you are.”

Fiji for Christ is part of a wider Seventh-day Adventist initiative known as OneVoice27, or “Mission for All”, which is building towards a coordinated global evangelistic program in the second half of 2027.

But in Fiji, the idea has been translated into something much closer to home.

The campaign has been building quietly for months.

Since January, local Adventist churches have conducted health checks, food demonstrations, health-juice exhibitions and Bible seminars. The smaller programs provided opportunities to learn what worked, what needed improvement and what would be required to manage an undertaking on a national scale.

There were also periods of fasting and regular prayer, including Wednesday fasting and midday prayer sessions. Behind the public program is an organisational principle the Adventist Church calls Total Member Involvement.

It means the responsibility does not rest with a handful of pastors or church leaders. Members have been encouraged to take ownership of different aspects of the campaign — from preparing venues and assisting with health activities to welcoming visitors and following up those who ask for further information.

For Pastor Maika, that participation is central to the campaign’s purpose.

“To organise something this big will require unity within the church,” he says.

“When the church unites, we believe the whole of Fiji and its communities will unite too.”

It is an ambitious proposition in a country spread across hundreds of islands, with communities separated by distance, sea and geography.

The answer has been to build a program in which each location carries the same broad message while allowing local people to become the face of the campaign in their own communities.

At the centre of the operation will be a national command centre at the Adventist Church headquarters in Suvavou.

For the duration of the campaign, the headquarters will become more than an administrative office. It will function as the communications and coordination point for activities taking place across Fiji.

Reports from the various sites will be received each night. Visitor numbers, program updates and requests for further Bible study will be collated and passed between the field locations and the command centre. A toll-free number — 813 — will provide another channel for people seeking information or assistance.

The system is designed to give a national program a local rhythm: information gathered from villages, settlements, towns and islands can be relayed back to the centre, while instructions and logistical support can move in the opposite direction.

Fiji for Christ will involve 147 international speakers and 55 local speakers, delivering the nightly program from different locations around the country.

Yet behind those figures are thousands of volunteers and church members who will rarely be seen from the platform.

They will be arranging chairs, preparing children’s activities, helping with health checks, recording visitors, managing sound systems and ensuring that people who walk through the doors are received warmly.

item.title: DISCOVERING FIJI I Where Tailevu’s memories still live
item.description: FOR decades, Tailevu Hotel has stood through changing times, carrying the memories of families, travellers and generations who have passed through its doors. There is something about an old building that refuses to let the past disappear. In the dining area of Tailevu Hotel, the old-world character of the building still lingers.
item.content:encoded:
FOR decades, Tailevu Hotel has stood through changing times, carrying the memories of families, travellers and generations who have passed through its doors.

There is something about an old building that refuses to let the past disappear. In the dining area of Tailevu Hotel, the old-world character of the building still lingers.

Its colonial feel and craftsmanship carry a sense of another time – when dairy farmers gathered after a day’s work, express buses stopped along the old Kings Road and families travelled between Suva and Tailevu.

The hotel is more than a building in Korovou. It is part of the memory of Tailevu North. For Oliver Williams, director of Tailevu Hotel, its story begins in the 1950s when William Gatward designed and built the hotel on land belonging to the Mataqali Tuicolo of Matacaucau Village, Tailevu North. Gatward was the hotel’s original owner and proprietor.

The hotel became a place where some of the area’s pioneering dairy families, the Gatwards, Harrisons, Scotts and Harnesses – could gather and socialise.

“These families were the pioneers of the dairy industry in Tailevu North,” Williams said.

It was a different Tailevu then, and the hotel became woven into the rhythm of life in the area.

The old Kings Road brought another kind of visitor to the hotel.

Express buses travelling along the road would stop at Tailevu Hotel, giving passengers time to get off, use the toilet, stretch their legs and buy food and refreshments before continuing their journey.

For Kuila Kaci, Williams’ mother, those stops became part of childhood. She remembers travelling to and from Suva as a little girl and stopping at the hotel. Years later, her connection to the place would become much deeper.

The hotel was closely connected to the Gatward family, whose former farm and residence is in Deepwater.

Williams said the architecture of the former Gatward residence is like the hotel. The Gatwards and Harnesses became well known in the area, their names becoming part of the landscape of Tailevu North.

Gatward Park, beside Tailevu North College carries the name of William Gatward. The hotel, too, carried his mark.

At some point, Gokals took over Tailevu Hotel while the Tailevu Provincial Council was involved in what Williams described as some form of partnership.

Then, in 1992 the hotel changed hands again. Warick Williams and Kuila Kaci, through Ryda Limited (now known as Ryda Proprietary Limited) bought the property from Gokal.

What they found was a building that had lost much of its former character.

“Renovations started soon after settlement. The property was run down and a shadow of its former glory,” Williams said.

Instead, the family relied on hurricane lamps and an old British generator for light and power.

For the children, however the lack of electricity brought its own kind of excitement.

“As kids this was fun and exciting. Our mother hated it!” Williams recalled.

The family set about renovating the property.

But restoring the building would prove to be only one chapter in its changing story.

After the renovations, Ryda Proprietary Ltd leased the entire premises to Subash, the owner of Kings Hotel in Nausori. The hotel became a nightclub and watering hole.

And with that came another side of its history.

There were fights and clashes between rival villages. One night, a massive brawl erupted between young men from Naivicula and Navunisole.

The violence left considerable damage behind. Windows were broken. Steel doors were ripped from their hinges. The hotel was almost set on fire.

Many people were injured. Korovou police eventually brought the chaos under control.

The incident occurred only a month after the hotel had been leased to Subash. The lease was immediately cancelled.

Subash returned to the safety of Nausori. Yet the hotel’s association with nightlife continued.

At some point, the Bull & Bell nightclub was established. It became famous or infamous, depending on who was asked – among locals and travellers.

item.title: COMMUNITY I Taking the Bula spirit to the world
item.description: FOR Fiji, the Road to Serbia is about more than travelling overseas, it is an opportunity to tell the country’s story, showcase its people and culture, and give young Fijians a place on the international stage. Youth and Sports Minister Jese Saukuru launched the Road to Serbia: Fiji’s Expo 2027 Belgrade Initiative during the Navosa Youth Festival, describing Fiji’s participation in the specialised
item.content:encoded:
FOR Fiji, the Road to Serbia is about more than travelling overseas, it is an opportunity to tell the country’s story, showcase its people and culture, and give young Fijians a place on the international stage.

Youth and Sports Minister Jese Saukuru launched the Road to Serbia: Fiji’s Expo 2027 Belgrade Initiative during the Navosa Youth Festival, describing Fiji’s participation in the specialised expo as an opportunity to share the country’s story with the world.

Expo 2027 Belgrade will be held in Serbia from May 15 to August 15, 2027, under the global theme “Playing for Humanity. Sport and Music for All”.

Fiji will participate under its national pavilion theme, “Bula Spirit, Play, Connect, Thrive”.

For Saukuru, the words capture values that are central to Fiji.

“We value connection, we value community, we value our culture, we value sport, we value creativity, and we value the relationships that bring people together,” he said.

The Government has supported Fiji’s participation in Expo 2027, which will provide a platform for the country to showcase its tourism, culture, sporting excellence, creative industries and youth development.

But the opportunities extend beyond visibility.

The expo is expected to open doors for stronger international partnerships, trade and investment, new opportunities for Fijians and greater cultural connections.

For Saukuru, young people will be an important part of that journey.

“Importantly, our young people will be part of the journey – our young people on the world stage,” he said.

The Road to Serbia initiative is intended to create pathways for young Fijians to connect with the world, showcase their abilities and play their part in representing Fiji internationally.

Saukuru said young people had talent, creativity, sporting ability, business ideas and stories to share.

“You have something unique to offer,” he said.

He urged young Fijians not to allow their place of origin to limit their ambitions.

“Do not limit your dreams because of where you come from,” he said.

“Dream beyond your village, dream beyond your school, dream beyond your community, believe in your talent, believe in your ability, and believe that your skills and your hard work can take you places you may never have imagined.”

Yet, as young Fijians look towards the world beyond their communities, Saukuru reminded them to carry their origins with them.

“Wherever your journey takes you, never forget where you come from,” he said.

“Carry your culture with pride, carry your values with pride and most importantly, carry the Bula spirit with you.”

According to the Road to Serbia guide, Expo 2027 Belgrade is a specialised expo recognised by the Bureau International des Expositions (BIE).

It will provide Fiji with a platform to showcase its identity, build partnerships and create lasting impact for its people and their future.

The expo is expected to attract more than four million visitors, with more than 120 countries expected to participate.

It will also be the first specialised expo hosted in the Western Balkans.

Participating countries are expected to use the expo for national visibility, economic diplomacy, innovation exchange, culture and creativity, education and youth, and the promotion of a sustainable future.

For Fiji, the participation aligns with national priorities of building a resilient economy, empowering its people and strengthening the country’s place in the world.

It will also provide an opportunity to showcase Fiji’s uniqueness and values.

Fiji’s vision for Expo 2027 is to showcase the essence of the country, its people, culture and potential – while building meaningful connections that create opportunities for a better tomorrow.

At the centre of Fiji’s participation will be its national pavilion, designed to provide a vibrant and immersive experience that brings the heart of Fiji to Belgrade.

The pavilion theme, “Bula Spirit, Play, Connect, Thrive”, will provide the framework for telling Fiji’s story.
